name: traversal that inherently covers every element (for-each) vs. indexed loop whose bound comes from the *other* list
side_a: Do not deduct when the candidate reaches the elements by iterating the list itself — an enhanced for-each over `historyList` (and/or `mathList`), or an indexed loop whose bound is that same list's own `size()`. Such traversal inherently touches every element, so the 'accesses all elements' point is earned.
side_b: Deduct when the index used to access one list is bounded by a different list's size (e.g., `for (int i = 0; i < mathList.size(); i++) { ... historyList.get(i) ... }`), since the access is only valid under an unstated parallel-lists assumption and is not guaranteed to visit every element of the accessed list.

name: Direct instance-variable/array access substituted for accessor calls vs. actual method invocation on a CourseRecord element
side_a: No_deduct when the student actually invokes the accessors with call syntax on a CourseRecord element (e.g., `hist.getStudentID()`, `math.getAbsences()`), regardless of how the element was obtained (enhanced for-loop, indexed `get(i)`, nested loops) or whether the surrounding comparison logic (`>=`, `==` on Strings, missing break) is correct.
side_b: Deduct when the response reaches the data by naming the private fields directly or by array syntax instead of calling the methods — e.g., `historyList[i].studentID`, `mathList[j].absences`, `historyList.length` — since no invocation of getStudentID/getAbsences ever appears, even though the intent is clear and the element referenced is a CourseRecord.

name: operator must be strict `>` vs. any relational operator on absences counts
side_a: deduct if the only absences comparison in the response uses a non-strict or non-ordering operator (`>=`, `<=`, `==`, `!=`); 'more history than math absences' requires a strict greater-than, so `hist.getAbsences() >= math.getAbsences()` does not earn the point.
side_b: no_deduct if the response compares the two absences values with any relational operator that distinguishes magnitude, treating `>=` as a trivial off-by-one that still shows the intended comparison.

name: absence values must actually be accessed and compared vs. matching students alone suffices
side_a: deduct if the response never retrieves the absences values (no `getAbsences()`/`.absences` access) and instead only matches student IDs and increments a counter, since no absences comparison exists at all.
side_b: no_deduct if the response identifies the matching student pairs, treating the ID match plus counting as implicitly addressing the comparison requirement.

name: Student IDs compared with .equals() vs compared with == (reference equality)
side_a: No deduction if the response matches records by comparing the String student IDs with .equals() (e.g., `hist.getStudentID().equals(math.getStudentID())`), which is a valid String comparison.
side_b: Deduct if the response matches records by comparing String student IDs with `==`, which compares references rather than String contents and so does not reliably identify the same student.

name: Actually compares the two absence counts vs only tests for a matching student
side_a: No deduction if, after matching a student in both lists, the response compares the two absence values (e.g., `hist.getAbsences() >= math.getAbsences()`) before incrementing the counter.
side_b: Deduct if the response increments the counter merely because the student appears in both lists, never retrieving or comparing absence counts.
